research_rationale: EO 8179 (Franklin D. Roosevelt, signed June 21, 1939; 4 FR 2468) was read in full in the held Federal Register text jobs/fr-originals/data/full_run/texts/EO_8179.txt, the text layer of the official govinfo PDF; its closing line reads '[No. 8179]' and its heading is Amending Certain Provisions of the Civil Service Rules. It amends three provisions of the Civil Service Rules: Rule IX section 2 (reinstatement of probationers), Rule X section 6(a) (the absolute-appointment condition for transfer) and Rule XI section 1(a) and (b) (promotion during probation). The first end of every clause is the express revocation by EO 9830, effective May 1, 1947. EO 9830 Part II restates the Civil Service Rules as a whole; Part III is a separate sentence revoking listed orders by number and date. Part III contains no exception, saving or transition wording, and nothing else in the held text of EO 9830 names this order. The dossier's later-event chain for this order holds one event, EO 9830, and the OFR disposition notes found by the bounded search name EO 9830 as revoking it. The U.S. Code search (edition through 2026-10-09) and the eCFR search (as of 2026-10-14) found no citation of this order. The dossier's notes record that a later order restated Rule X section 6(a) and added a subdivision to Rule IX section 2, and that other wartime and 1946 provisions touched probation and transfer; that text is not attached to this packet as evidence. Under the owner's 2026-10-21 strike-and-insert ruling a restatement continues the amended clause until the parent order ends, so it is a later amendment and not an end, and no held source shows that any earlier instrument extinguished a clause of this order. The represented text is the Federal Register text layer, not a page image; the page images were not examined.

It amends three rules: Rule I section 1 (no interference with elections), Rule XII section 5 (retention of soldiers and sailors in reductions in force) and Rule XV (legal appointment necessary to compensation), and ends with the sentence 'This order shall be effective as of' November 7, 1940. That retroactive effective date is the start of the order's operation; it is not an end. The first end of every clause is the express revocation by EO 9830, effective May 1, 1947. Part III of EO 9830 lists 'No. 8705 of March 6, 1941.' The held text of EO 8705 is dated March 5, 1941 at the White House and was filed March 6, 1941, so the list gives the filing date of the same numbered order; the number identifies it, and no other order of that number exists. EO 9830 Part II restates the Civil Service Rules as a whole; Part III revokes listed orders in a separate sentence and has no exception, saving or transition wording. The dossier's later-event chain for this order holds one event, EO 9830, and the OFR disposition notes found by the bounded search name EO 9830 as revoking it. The U.S. Code search (edition through 2026-10-09) and the eCFR search (as of 2026-10-14) found no citation of this order. A later restatement of any of the three rules, if one exists, would continue the clause amended under the owner's 2026-10-21 strike-and-insert ruling and is not an end; none is attached to this packet as evidence. research_rationale: EO 9301 (Franklin D. Roosevelt, signed February 9, 1943; 8 FR 1825, issue of February 11, 1943) was read in full in the held Federal Register text jobs/fr-originals/data/full_run/texts/EO_9301.txt, the text layer of the official govinfo PDF; its heading is Establishing a Minimum Wartime Workweek of Forty-Eight Hours and it is filed as F.R. Doc. 43-2162 on February 10, 1943. Its operative text is five numbered sections: section 1 ('For the duration of the war' no plant or place of employment is deemed to make the most effective use of manpower if its minimum workweek is under 48 hours; the machine inventory holds it inside the lead row because the OCR prints its number as 'J.'), section 2 (agencies require contractors to comply), section 3 (the Chairman of the War Manpower Commission interprets, issues regulations and may set a greater or lesser minimum workweek), section 4 (agencies comply with the Chairman's regulations) and section 5 (rule of construction preserving other hours and wage laws and the Fair Labor Standards Act). The first end of every clause is the express revocation by EO 9607 (Harry S. Truman, signed August 30, 1945; 10 FR 11191), whose whole operative text is the sentence ordering 'Executive Order 9301 of February 9,' 1943 'it is hereby, revoked.' The order says nothing about a delayed effective date, the order was signed on August 30, 1945 and filed the same day (11:41 a.m.), so the end is August 30, 1945. 'For the duration of the war' in section 1 is not an earlier own-terms end on this record: no held source states when the war's duration ended, and the express revocation of August 30, 1945 is the only held instrument that ends the clause. The OFR disposition notes name EO 9607 as revoking this order and also record cross-references from EO 9333 and EO 9332 (dated April 1943). The held text of EO 9332, printed on 8 FR 5355 in the issue of April 24, 1943, recites that the War Manpower Commission Chairman issues regulations under EO 9301; it is a recital of continuing authority, not a revocation, supersession or amendment. The dossier's EO 9600 lead text (10 FR 10166, issue of August 21, 1945) prints a War Manpower Commission rescission of the Commission's own Regulation No. 3 (Part 903, Minimum Wartime Workweek of 48 Hours) by its Chairman under EOs 9139, 9279 and 9301. That is an act of the Chairman under section 3 on his implementing regulation, not a revocation or supersession of this order, and it is not shown to have extinguished any command of the order; that lead text is not cited as a source here and was not confirmed as a working text.
savings_reason: EO 9607 consists of the revocation sentence and contains no saving, exception or transition wording. Obligations that contractors incurred under contracts made while EO 9301 and the Commission's regulations were in force arise from those contracts and regulations, not from a continuing command of the order, and no held source shows any continuing effect of the order after August 30, 1945. Section 5 preserved other hours and wage laws, which are independent of the order.
earlier_end_check: Own terms: section 1 is limited 'For the duration of the war', but no held source dates the end of the war's duration, so there is no own-terms end to record. Earlier instruments: the held later-event chain shows EO 9607 as the revoking order; the OFR cross-references from EO 9332 and EO 9333 are recitals of the Chairman's authority and not revocations. A rescission by the Chairman of the War Manpower Commission of his Regulation No. 3 in August 1945 ended that regulation, not the President's order; no held source shows it extinguished sections 1 to 5. EO 9607 names the order by number and date and revokes it on signing.
scope_check: The inventory has five rows covering the whole operative text: the lead row (authority and purposes, with section 1 as its last sentence) and sections 2, 3, 4 and 5. The signature block is not operative. Section 1's content is addressed in the lead row's reason.
independent_command_check: No clause survives the order independently. Sections 2 to 4 direct agencies and contractors to follow the minimum workweek and the Chairman's regulations; section 3 authorizes the Chairman to vary the workweek and issue regulations; section 5 is a rule of construction about other laws and the Fair Labor Standards Act and has no force apart from the order. None is a one-time act with a separate end date.
